newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: PLDT says rivals' complaints unfair.
newsitem.headline: PLDT says rivals' complaints unfair.

text.p: The Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co (PLDT), which enjoyed a virtual monopoly for decades until the government forced it to accept competition, now complains it is getting a raw deal from its smaller rivals.
New companies that have formed in the four years since the Philippines opened up the sector are complaining that PLDT is too slow in carrying out interconnection agreements.
PLDT says this is unfair and that it is moving as fast as it can.

"It is a misunderstanding on the part of some, that this problem is 100 percent caused by PLDT, which is not fair," senior vice president, corporate services group, Antonio Samson told Reuters in an interview on Monday.
PLDT owns the main highway on which the country's telecommunications traffic runs. For other companies to operate at all, they must have access to the main highway.
Few rivals have been prepared to come out in the open with their complaints for fear of damaging their relations with PLDT.

But last month, Bayan Telecommunications Holdings Corp (Bayantel), a unit of Benpres Holdings Corp, formally complained to the National Telecommunications Communications (NTC) that PLDT was dragging its heels.
The NTC urged PLDT to speed up its interconnection agreements and on Monday, the two companies said they had agreed on an interim solution to their differences.
PLDT says part of the problem is that its competitors have not clearly said how much traffic they expect to generate.
If the new companies want to connect to PLDT's highway, "the highway has to be broadened to accommodate all these connections," Samson said.

"That's why we have to know how many cars are going to pass our highway. Are they going north or south? All we are asking for is, let's plan jointly so that we know how many lanes to add to our highway," he added.
Despite the complaints, PLDT said it was not overly concerned about its new competition, saying the market as a whole was growing so quickly it can accommodate the new players.
"Our share of the pie may be going down, but the pie is growing at a fast rate," Samson said.
There were other benefits as well, he said. The telecommunications boom meant PLDT could raise funds in international markets at much more attractive terms.
"Earlier, ours was seen as a one-company industry," he said.
With more firms in the market, suppliers also have better economies of scale and offer better prices, he said.
"The cost per line has therefore been coming down."
From 1993 until June this year, PLDT spent over $2.6 billion on expansion, and expects to raise a further $2 billion starting in the first quarter of next year, he said.
And there is much more room for growth. The Philippines now has just two telephones per 100 people compared to 30 per 100 people in developed countries.
Investors appear to agree with PLDT's assessments. Its shares rose 60 pesos ($2.29) to close at 1,695 pesos ($64.69) in Manila on Tuesday.
"PLDT is still the best telecom bet among local telephone carriers because of its extensive network," said Fritz Aclan, research head at Dharmala Securities.
